title: B.C. municipal elections: Polls close in less than an hour as voters choose next mayors, councillors

image.caption: Signage in Vancouver on Oct. 7, the second day of advance voting. (Nav Rahi/CBC)

blocks.text: Voters in 161 B.C. municipalities go to the polls to elect their next mayor and council, school board and, in some cases, park board. Join hosts Lien Yeung and Stephen Quinn along with Jason D'Souza, Chris Walker and Justin McElroy for live coverage and analysis as results come in from from across the province.

items: Millions of British Columbians are choosing their next local governments today, with voting open in municipalities across the province.
More than 3,500 candidates are running across 189 local bodies in B.C., including municipalities and regional districts.
Heading into election day, local leaders were worried about confusion and low turnout given the provincial election takes place a week from today.
Polls close provincewide at 8 p.m. local time.

October 18Surrey candidates weigh new facilities and housing growthAkshay KulkarniSurrey mayor says $360M Vancouver Giants arena will be built on timeThe City of Surrey plans to build a 10,000-seat hockey arena that will be the new home of the WHL's Vancouver Giants. Surrey Mayor Brenda Locke defended the project, and said it would not lead to unnecessary costs for taxpayers while Giants majority owner Ron Toigo says the team will not immediately move to rename itself the Surrey Giants.Surrey's mayoral candidates have promised a range of new community and recreation facilities if elected, including a waterfront district, a conference centre and new pools.Building community infrastructure to serve Surrey's burgeoning population has been a big issue for years, with a 10,000-seat arena the latest major facility to be greenlit — even as the cost of the police transition weighs on the city's budget.The major candidates, however, have different ideas on how they'll balance housing and population growth to go along with those large projects.Locke says she will build on her work in the past, including approving more than 13,800 net new units.Annis and McCallum, meanwhile, are pushing back on the province's push for more dense housing centred around public transit. Annis says infrastructure needs to keep up with growth, while McCallum is pushing for the Crescent Beach and Ocean Park areas to be excluded from provincial housing legislation.Starchuk has promised to build more affordable homes on city land, with priority for family-sized homes.Troy Van Vliet is promising a family housing policy to include targets for two- and three-bedroom homes, while Honveer Randhawa says he would guarantee that building permits for single-family homes and renovations stamped by authorized firms are issued within five business days.

Race to watch: Locke and McCallum face off again in SurreyAkshay KulkarniWho will be the next mayor of Surrey?CBC’s The Early Edition brought together five candidates vying to be mayor of Surrey for two debates: Mike Starchuk with Imagine Surrey, Surrey city councillor Linda Annis, incumbent mayor Brenda Locke, Conservative Party of Surrey candidate Honveer Randhawa and Troy Van Vilet, a Surrey builder and business owner.Much like in Vancouver, former council allies are competing for the mayoral role in Surrey, B.C.'s second-largest city by population and one whose population growth rate led Canada for many years.Incumbent Brenda Locke of Surrey Connect was formerly a councillor under Doug McCallum, the city's mayor between 2018 and 2022 who is now running again with the Safe Surrey Coalition.The pair split in 2019 over McCallum's support for an independent Surrey Police Service (SPS), with Locke preferring to stay with the Surrey RCMP.With that issue now largely in the rearview mirror — the province having ordered the transition to the SPS — Locke and McCallum join a crowded field as they aim for the city's top job once again.Among those on the list are Coun. Linda Annis, who leads the Surrey First slate, and former MLA and councillor Mike Starchuk, leader of the Imagine Surrey slate.Two candidates — Honveer Randhawa of the Conservative Electors Association and Troy Van Vliet of Surrey Now — haven't held elected office before.

Property taxes a key issue in VancouverAkshay KulkarniVancouver Mayor Ken Sim promises tax freeze and community centres if re-electedVancouver Mayor Ken Sim made his final State of the City address for his first term to the Board of Trade on Wednesday, and with it came two big election promises. Justin McElroy reports on what the mayor is putting front and centre in his platform. Sim swept to power with a super-majority in 2022 on the back of a campaign largely focused on public safety.After four years as mayor, Sim is now promising a property tax freeze if an ABC majority is elected, after the 2026 budget featured one, too.All the other major candidates in the race have slammed that move and Sim's promise, with Fry saying the budgeted property tax freeze led to major cutbacks in city services and administration. Fry has promised more accessible, line-item budgets if he's elected.Allam has promised to cap property tax increases to the rate of inflation, while Hardwick is also promising "predictable increases" in line with inflation.Bligh has promised to replace the property tax freeze with increases based on long-term planning.

Race to watch: Vancouver mayoral race features 5 main slatesAkshay KulkarniVancouver’s mayoral field shifts into focusAfter a week where two Vancouver mayoral candidates left the race, voters are getting a clearer sense of the main choices on the ballot next month. As the CBC's Justin McElroy reports, they’re all trying to position themselves in slightly different ways.The leaders of five major political slates are aiming to be mayor of B.C.'s most populous city.They include the incumbent, Ken Sim of ABC Vancouver, and his former chief of staff, Kareem Allam, who is running for the Vancouver Liberals.Two longtime councillors — Pete Fry of the Vancouver Greens, and Rebecca Bligh of Vote Vancouver — are also in the race, as is former councillor Colleen Hardwick of TEAM Vancouver.Bligh was kicked out of ABC Vancouver last year while Hardwick ran for council in 2018 with Sim, who was then the NPA's mayoral candidate.Fry was the only opposition voice in the previous council for a period of time due to councillor vacancies and an ABC super-majority.

What does a local government do?Arden McLeodWhat municipalities can and can’t do in B.C.With municipal and provincial elections going on at the same time, it can be hard to know which promises being made at the local level are realistic, and which ones aren’t. The CBC’s Justin McElroy explains what powers cities actually have.Many major funding and policy decisions sit with the province and its ministries. But Kimberly Speers, who teaches public administration at UVic, says people can feel the impact of local government decisions every day."It's not generally seen as, you know, an exciting part of governing ... but at the same time, my gosh, are those local services so, so important," Speers said.Municipalities like Vancouver tend to spend the most on protective services, such as police, fire, and emergency services.Another big ticket item for municipalities is utilities like water, sewage and waste. Municipalities also oversee parks, recreation and culture centres and how land-use is determined — as well as maintaining sidewalks, roads and public transportation.

Multiple votes to cast in civic electionsArden McLeodElection overload is real in B.C. ahead of 2 back-to-back votesElection overload is real in B.C. with 2 back-to-back votesMunicipal political parties generally don't map neatly onto provincial parties across B.C., and depending on where you live, polling can include elections for bodies like school boards, as well as for mayor and council.In Vancouver, for instance, residents are voting for one mayor, 10 city councillors, seven park board commissioners and nine school board trustees.In provincial elections, on the other hand, voters simply choose one candidate to represent their riding in the legislature.

Record number of advance voters in some municipalitiesAkshay KulkarniA cyclist heading toward an advance voting station in Vancouver. (Nav Rahi/CBC)Vancouver is among many municipalities that saw a record number of residents make use of advance voting opportunities for this election.The city says 103,000 voters cast a ballot over four advance voting days, smashing a record of 65,127 in 2022. Officials also say mail-in voting requests doubled compared to 2022, with 21,000 requests this year.Surrey and Kelowna, among others, also saw high advance voter turnouts.Every municipality was required to provide at least one advance voting day in B.C.That's encouraging because, despite a local government's major impact on voters' lives — given they are usually responsible for day-to-day services like garbage collection, sewage and policing — voter turnout in B.C.'s civic elections are usually lower than provincial and federal elections.In 2022, 29.2 per cent of eligible voters cast a ballot, well below the turnout for the subsequent provincial and federal elections, according to CivicInfoBC.

It's election night in British Columbia – the 1st of 2Rhianna SchmunkA voting sign in Vancouver on Oct. 7. (Nav Rahi/CBC)British Columbians are choosing their next local representatives on councils, school boards and other regional posts on Saturday, the first of two election days this month.The Union of B.C. Municipalities says more than 3,500 local government candidates are running across 189 local bodies in B.C., which include municipalities and regional districts. CBC's Decision Desk will be closely following the vote count after polls close across most of the province at 8 p.m. local time, and will deliver projections of the results in some of B.C.'s biggest communities, including Kamloops, Kelowna, Richmond, Surrey, Vancouver and Victoria.The overlapping provincial election had many worried about widespread voter confusion. Still, many cities and municipalities reported increased or even record turnout at advance polls, including Vancouver, Richmond, Burnaby, Kamloops, Surrey, Kelowna, Prince George, Cranbrook and View Royal.Voters will cast their ballots again next Saturday for the provincial election.
